one_liner: Go rewrite of Miller, the header-keyed CSV/JSON record tool; beats its C predecessor 5.10.3 on CSV and multi-verb chains.
what_it_does: mlr is a command-line tool in the spirit of awk, sed, cut, join and sort for name-indexed records: it reads CSV, TSV, JSON, DKVP, NIDX, XTAB and other formats, runs a then-chain of verbs (cat, sort, stats1, put and filter with Miller's own DSL, and many more) and writes any of those formats. Miller 6 replaces the C Miller 5 as the same mlr binary, but it is not fully backward compatible: the docs keep a list of changes from Miller 5 in flags, types and DSL behaviour. It is a CLI, not a library API.
how_it_is_fast: Miller 6 runs the reader as two goroutines (byte reading and record building), each verb of the then-chain as its own goroutine and the writer as another, connected by channels that pass batches of records (--records-per-batch); C Miller 5 runs the whole chain on one core. A four-put chain therefore spreads over several cores (cpu.md: at most 250-350 percent CPU for deep chains), which explains most of the 4.7x chain-4 gap, and even a single verb overlaps parsing, the verb and formatting. The June 2026 work cut heap allocations per record and field (lazy per-record hashing, slab allocation of record fields, writer-buffer reuse, DSL stack-frame pooling and copy elision). The docs give no mechanism for the CSV reader gain over Miller 5.
when_to_use: Multi-step transformations of header-keyed CSV, TSV or JSON in a shell pipeline (cut, sort, stats1, put or filter joined with then) on a machine with idle cores, where reader, verbs and writer can run in parallel.
Replacing Miller 5: in the 2026-02-22 M1 run, then-chains of put ran about 2.4x (one put) to 4.7x (four puts) faster, stats1 about 2x, CSV cat about 1.9x and XTAB cat about 2.9x (read from charts).
Format conversion between CSV, TSV, JSON, DKVP and XTAB where header handling, quoting and heterogeneous records matter more than peak throughput.
When one dependency-free binary must run on Linux, macOS and Windows (apt, yum, snap, brew, port, choco, winget and scoop packages per the README).
when_not_to_use: Single fixed operations on big files: on the page's own 40-million-record cell_towers.csv, mlr cut took 1m27.6s real and 3m8.9s user against 1m8.3s real and 1m7.1s user for the M1 laptop's system cut; in issue #1527 Miller 6.11.0 cut on a 5 GB CSV was killed after 2:15.86 while qsv select took 3.988 s (6.12.0 finished in 12:45.40).
JSON or NIDX heavy work if you still have Miller 5: in the 2026-02-22 run Miller 6.17.0 took about 8.7 s vs 6.3 s on JSON cat and about 3.2 s vs 0.9 s on NIDX cat.

Data larger than RAM through non-streaming verbs: sort and tac keep every record in memory and do not spill to disk (sort -nf peaked at 1306 MB RSS on the one-million-record CSV after the June 2026 work).

Core-starved settings (single-CPU containers, many concurrent mlr processes, GOMAXPROCS=1): the chain advantage depends on spare cores, and Miller 6 spends more total CPU than single-threaded C tools.

Peak CSV throughput: catalogued tools such as qsv, xan, zsv, tsv-utils, hck and tuc are built for speed on fixed operations, and the maintainer says xsv is known to be faster and Miller makes no claim to beat it.

integration.form: static binary (CLI); Go module github.com/johnkerl/miller/v6, executable built from cmd/mlr
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (README: zero runtime dependencies); building needs a Go toolchain
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.26.0 per go.mod at HEAD (go.mod at v6.17.0, the version in the 2026-02-22 charts, says go 1.24.0)
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (distribution packages listed in the README); all published 2026 timings are from one Apple M1 MacBook Air
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable to a CLI; internally one goroutine per reader stage, verb and writer, with core use controlled by GOMAXPROCS
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same mlr command and verb set as Miller 5, but Miller 6 changed some flags, type handling and DSL behaviour (documented list of changes from Miller 5); not a drop-in for awk, cut or sort

gotchas: Wall clock hides extra CPU: all Miller 5 versus Miller 6 numbers are elapsed time against single-threaded C, and the charts give no user time. The page's one user-time sample (mlr cut 3m8.9s user vs system cut 1m7.1s user on the same file) shows Miller 6 using about 2.8x the CPU of a C tool for the same column extraction (derived from page data).

Harness: scripts/perf/time-verbs.py launches each case through the shell with output to /dev/null, averages 5 runs, and neither checks the exit status nor compares output between versions, so a failing or semantically different run would still be timed. The Miller 5 binary's build (autotools default -g -O2) and the Go compiler version for the 2026 runs are not stated.

Do not mix the page's two runs: the June 2026 table is best-of-five for 6.18.1 versus 6.19.0, while the 2026-02-22 charts average five runs for 5.10.3 through 6.17.0. CSV cat was 0.62 s 'before' in June against about 0.8 s for 6.17.0 in February, so June figures cannot be set against the Miller 5 points.

Regressions inside Miller 6: NIDX cat went from about 0.9 s at 6.0.0 to 2.7 s at 6.8.0 and 3.2 s at 6.17.0 in the same chart, and 6.0.0 had sort -n at about 6 s and JSON cat at about 16 s before later fixes. Issue #1409 reports mlr count on a 5 GB CSV killed while wc -l finished in 37.9 s; the maintainer closed it saying slower-than-wc is expected.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Miller when you need format-aware, header-keyed processing across CSV, TSV, JSON and DKVP with a DSL and multi-verb chains in one binary. For a single fixed operation the siblings are faster: hck and tuc beat cut by about 4.6-6.3x and 5.3x, eBay tsv-utils beats awk and cut, while Miller's own page shows it slower than system cut.
verified_claims_summary: First-party wall-clock times read from PNG charts dated 2026-02-22 (Apple M1 MacBook Air, average of 5 shell-launched runs per case by scripts/perf/time-verbs.py, one-million-record files): Miller 6.17.0 (Go) against Miller 5.10.3 (C, build flags not stated), put chain-1 about 1.6 s vs 3.8 s, chain-4 about 2.15 s vs 10.2 s, stats1 about 0.9 s vs 1.8 s, CSV cat about 0.8 s vs 1.5 s, but NIDX cat about 3.2 s vs 0.9 s and JSON cat about 8.7 s vs 6.3 s. The baseline is Miller's own C predecessor, not awk, cut or sort, and the big wins come from running the pipeline on several cores.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-29, 10.0k stars, packaged by the major Linux distributions, Homebrew and Windows package managers) and BSD-2-Clause, but the speed evidence is first-party, chart-only and against its own single-threaded C predecessor, so read it as 'the Go rewrite wins on CSV and deep chains through pipelining' rather than as Go beating C.
